title: Real AI Agents Need Planning, Not Just Prompting - Yuval Belfer
talk_summary: Yuval Belfer argues that complex agent tasks need explicit planning plus an execution engine that analyzes step dependencies, enables parallel execution, and trades off speed vs cost, rather than pure ReAct step-by-step prompting. He shows AI21's Maestro separating context/task/requirements, generating multiple candidates (best-of-N), pruning by budget, validating and iterating, with modest quality gains at higher runtime and cost.

takeaways.technique: Separate plan from execution with dependency-aware parallel steps
takeaways.what_they_do: A planner produces the step graph, and an execution engine analyzes dependencies between steps so independent steps run in parallel instead of one-at-a-time ReAct loops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an execution engine can analyze dependencies between steps which enables par parallel execution

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of committing to one plan end-to-end, the agent periodically asks whether the current plan is still good and replans if not.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in the middle you can ask yourself is this plan good or should I do planning and go somewhere else

takeaways.what_they_do: Sample several candidates from one or different LLMs at high temperature, score them, and only continue improving the promising ones within a predefined budget.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we also ditch the candidates that do not seem like they will be good and only pursue the best candidate or candidates based on predefined budget
takeaways.numbers: Quality gains cited on IFEval and internal requirement-satisfaction set, at cost of 'more runtime and more money'.

takeaways.technique: Split context, task, and requirements into separate validated fields
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of shoving context, task, and constraints into one prompt, they are separated so each requirement can be validated independently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the thing that you usually just shove in the prompt. Now they are separated so it will be easier to validate

takeaways.what_they_do: The execution engine annotates candidate paths with expected cost, latency, and success probability, and the planner picks the path accordingly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the execution engine can say what is the expected cost the expected latency latency and success probability and the planner will choose accordingly

takeaways.technique: Start simple; escalate to planning only when task is complex
takeaways.what_they_do: Explicit guidance to use SLMs/tools/ReAct first and only add planner+execution engine for genuinely complex tasks needing parallelization and explainability.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I will always say start simple and then use whatever work. So if you can use SLMs use SLMs
